name: Childhood vaccinations: the NHS schedule
summary: The NHS offers babies and children vaccines against many serious illnesses, from 8 weeks old through school, and a GP surgery can arrange any that are missed.
keyPoints: The NHS lists routine childhood vaccines by age, starting with the babies' visits at 8, 12 and 16 weeks.
From 1 January 2026 the MMRV vaccine, which adds chickenpox protection, replaced MMR in the routine schedule for children.
Older children are offered HPV in Year 8, and MenACWY and the 3-in-1 teenage booster in Year 9, according to UKHSA and NHS pages.
The NHS says it is best to have vaccines on time, but most can still be caught up if missed, and a GP surgery can arrange this.
Redness or swelling where the needle went in and a fever are common after vaccines, and a young baby with a high temperature is a reason to contact the GP urgently.

body.heading: Which vaccines does the NHS offer in the first year?
body.body: The NHS lists the routine vaccines by age, and its table starts with the babies' visits at 8, 12 and 16 weeks. The 6-in-1 vaccine helps protect against six serious illnesses: diphtheria, hepatitis B, Hib, polio, tetanus and whooping cough. The GOV.UK schedule for 1 July 2026 places rotavirus and MenB vaccines at the early visits, and the pneumococcal vaccine at 16 weeks. Rotavirus vaccine is for a stomach bug, MenB is for a type of meningitis bacteria, and the pneumococcal vaccine is named for the pneumococcus germ. The GOV.UK schedule lists the pneumococcal and MenB vaccines again at one year. The NHS page also covers extra vaccines for children in at-risk groups, such as those with long-term conditions or a weakened immune system.

body.heading: What is offered at 18 months and before school?
body.body: According to the NHS, children born on or after 1 July 2024 are offered a fourth dose of the 6-in-1 vaccine at 18 months. For those children the Hib/MenC vaccine was dropped, and the GOV.UK schedule no longer lists it. The NHS table also lists a pre-school booster against diphtheria, tetanus, whooping cough and polio at 3 years and 4 months. Children born before 1 July 2024 follow an earlier version of the schedule, so GOV.UK publishes a separate table for them.

body.heading: What changed with chickenpox and MMRV in 2026?
body.body: The MMRV vaccine protects against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox, and it was added to the routine schedule on 1 January 2026. NHS pages describe two doses, at 12 months and at 18 months, which brings the second measles, mumps and rubella dose forward from 3 years and 4 months. A catch-up offer of chickenpox vaccine for some older children is described on GOV.UK, but sources give different start dates. Scotland runs its own programme, and NHS inform gives a different timetable from England's.

body.heading: What is offered at school?
body.body: School teams offer HPV vaccine to boys and girls in Year 8, to protect against genital warts and cancers linked to HPV. The MenACWY vaccine and the 3-in-1 teenage booster, called Td/IPV, are offered in Year 9, although some areas say Year 9 or 10. The NHS says the children's flu vaccine is offered to 2 and 3 year olds, to pupils from reception to Year 11, and to children with certain long-term conditions. Most school-age children have it at school in the autumn term, and the usual form is a nasal spray. Children turning 18 move on to the adult injected flu vaccine, and some pharmacies may offer the vaccine to eligible children, with the NHS page setting out which. An injected version is offered if the spray is unsuitable, including for families who do not accept the pork gelatine in the spray. Common flu spray side effects listed by the NHS include a blocked or runny nose, loss of appetite, tiredness and headache.

body.heading: How are vaccines arranged, and what if one is missed?
body.body: The NHS says a GP surgery can book or rearrange a vaccination appointment. The NHS says it is best to have vaccines on time, but most can still be caught up if they are missed. For the 6-in-1 vaccine, the NHS says a child can still have it up to the age of 10. Children who miss school sessions can catch up at a community clinic or at the GP, and those who are home educated can be offered flu vaccine at a community clinic. Young people starting university are advised to check their MenACWY, MMR and HPV vaccines, and the NHS says a GP can still give MenACWY until the 25th birthday. For anything unclear about a child's own schedule, the NHS and GOV.UK pages that match the child's birth date apply.

body.heading: What side effects are common, and when should someone get advice?
body.body: The GOV.UK guide for babies says redness, swelling or tenderness where the injection was given is common, and it goes away without treatment. For the 6-in-1 vaccine, the NHS lists swelling or pain where the injection was given, a high temperature, tiredness and loss of appetite. Irritability and fever are also common, and fever is more likely when the MenB vaccine is given with other vaccines. Allergic reactions are very rare and usually start within minutes, and the people giving vaccines are trained to treat them straight away. For a serious one, called anaphylaxis, the sources say it happens about once in every million immunisations. NHS inform Scotland advises contacting the GP urgently if a baby under 3 months has a high temperature, or if a fever lasts 48 hours after vaccination. The NHS says a flu vaccination may be postponed if a child is unwell on the day.
